slides.title: ResNet Quantization Hands-on
slides.subtitle: From opening the OE to on-board verification
slides.notes: This is Lesson 3 of Chapter 2, Model Zoo: ResNet Quantization Hands-on. In the last lesson, we got a Sample running on the board, using a model that was already converted. In this lesson, we follow along and quantize ResNet-18 ourselves. We start by opening the OE, then set up the environment, write the YAML, compile, and read the complete logs. At the end, we put the artifacts back into the Sample and verify them on the board.

slides.title: Lesson Roadmap
slides.heading: This lesson follows the ==order of operations==
slides.lead: Open the OE, set up the environment, compile, then check artifacts and verify on the board.

cards.text: What the OE is; from image to container.

slides.notes: This lesson follows the order of the actual operations, in four steps. Step one, open the OE: what it is, and how to get from the image into the container. Step two, set up the environment: following the conversion directory, prepare the working directory, the YAML, and the calibration data. Step three, compile: we do the X5 and the S100 once each, and show you the complete logs. Step four, look at the artifacts and the similarity, then verify on the board and run an evaluation. Before we begin, let's spend a few minutes on the PTQ theory.

slides.title: Chapter 01
slides.heading: Theory Overview
slides.sub: Let us go through the PTQ theory first
slides.notes: Part one: let's go through the theory first.

slides.title: Five PTQ Stages
slides.heading: The ==five stages== of PTQ

scene.text: A reliable float model comes first, then quantization

steps.caption: Stage 1: the float model, exported to ONNX
Stage 2: validation, compared with PyTorch
Stage 3: prepare the calibration data
Stage 4: quantize and compile, once each for X5 and S100
Stage 5: evaluate accuracy, a demo of how to measure
Five PTQ stages: from the float model to on-board verification

slides.notes: PTQ, post-training quantization, has five stages. One, the float model: take the weights and export them to ONNX. Two, validation: compare against PyTorch, then check the operators. Three, calibration data: prepare a batch of representative inputs. Four, quantize and compile: calibrate, quantize, and compile, once for each of the two toolchains. Five, evaluation: compare accuracy on a dataset. In this lesson, we do stage four by hand, then come back to validation and evaluation.

slides.title: Input Compiled In
slides.heading: Preprocessing is ==compiled into the model==

steps.caption: What the board feeds the model is NV12
Color conversion: NV12 to the RGB used in training
Normalization: subtract the mean, multiply by scale
All of this is compiled into the model at conversion; the input type is set in the yaml
The mean and scale in the yaml are exactly for this
The second job: optimize, quantize, and compile into an INT8 model

slides.notes: Conversion has to solve two things. First, how the input is handled. The board feeds the model NV12, while during training the model took RGB. Color conversion, subtracting the mean, and multiplying by a scale factor are not done on the board. Instead, they are compiled into the model at conversion time, which is exactly what mean and scale in the yaml are for. Second, optimize, quantize, and compile the model into an INT8 model that the BPU can run.

slides.title: Two Toolchains
slides.heading: One ONNX, ==two toolchains==

scene.text: S100P (nash-m) · S600 (nash-p): same tool, same yaml; only mentioned in text in this lesson

steps.caption: The same ONNX has to go to two toolchains
X5: enter the X5 OE image
hb_mapper: checker first, then makertbin
Produces a .bin for the X5
S100: enter the S series OE image
hb_compile: one command
Produces an .hbm for the S100
One ONNX, two toolchains, two kinds of artifact

slides.notes: Both toolchains are installed in Docker images. The X5 uses hb_mapper: first checker to check the model, then makertbin to convert it. It produces a bin file; the march is bayes-e, and the input is a single packed NV12. The S series uses hb_compile, one command, and it produces an hbm file. The S100's march is nash-e, and the input is a split NV12, with Y and UV kept separate. The S100P and the S600 use the same tool and the same yaml, and we won't convert them in this lesson.

scene.label: Working directory

steps.caption: OE: the algorithm toolchain provided by D-Robotics
Not software you install, but a Docker image
The image has every tool needed for conversion
Each series has CPU and GPU images, with different versions
For PTQ the CPU image is enough; a GPU is an optional speed-up
docker run starts a container; run commands inside
The working directory is mounted in, with the same path as on the host
Artifacts are written back to the working directory and stay after the container exits
S series images are on a registry; docker login before pulling

slides.notes: The OE is the algorithm toolchain provided by D-Robotics. It is not a piece of software you install, but a Docker image. The image already has all the tools needed for conversion. The X5 and the S series each have their own image versions; within a series there are also CPU images and GPU images. For PTQ alone, the CPU image is enough; when a usable GPU is available, the GPU image can speed things up. To use it, you start a container with docker run and run your commands inside. Our working directory is mounted into the container, with the same path as on the host. The artifacts we compile are written straight back to this directory, and they are still there after the container exits. The S series images are on a registry, and before pulling them you first have to docker login with your own account.

slides.heading: X5: ==opening the OE==

blocks.label: ① Confirm the image is local

note.p: The image ID uniquely identifies it

blocks.label: ② Enter the container, check the version

slides.notes: Let's start with the OE for the X5. The first command, docker image inspect, confirms the image is available locally. It is a v1.2.8 server image, with a name that starts with local. The first part of the output is the image's unique ID, followed by the creation time. The second command uses docker run to enter the container and runs hb_mapper with the version option. The container prints: hb_mapper 1.24.3. Then we filter pip list: hbdk 3.49.15, horizon-nn 1.1.0. With these version numbers, the versions in the later logs can be matched up. The rm, entrypoint, and bash -c in the command are explained one by one on the next page.
slides.lead: Real run · the X5 image used in this lesson: local/rdk-x5-oe:v1.2.8-server (paths and user names hidden).

slides.title: The S100 OE
slides.heading: S100: ==opening the OE==

note.p: This lesson demos the GPU image; there is also …_cpu:v3.7.0; pulling needs docker login
Real output: the environment is not broken

blocks.label: ③ Read versions with pip list

note.p: The compile log prints them again at the start

slides.notes: Now the image for the S100. It comes from the D-Robotics registry, with s100 in its name, version v3.7.0. This lesson's demo uses the GPU image; the same version also has a CPU image, and for PTQ the CPU image is enough. As before, first docker image inspect, then enter the container. Here's a pitfall: hb_compile does not support a version option. The command returns no such option; this is the real output, not us breaking the environment. So the version has to be read with pip list. horizon_tc_ui 3.5.3, hbdk4 4.7.5, hmct-gpu 2.6.5. The start of the compile log later prints these versions again.

slides.title: docker run Options
slides.heading: docker run: ==one by one==

blocks.label: ① The form used in this lesson

note.p: With a graphics card you can add --gpus all (optional speed-up)

lines.text: --rm delete on exit · --user your own files
-v / -w  mount and enter the working directory
--gpus all: optional with NVIDIA GPU; not needed for S series

note.p: Same path inside and outside the container; a CPU image also works

lines.text: i keeps input open · t allocates a terminal

note.p: This lesson uses one-shot commands; logs are easier to save

slides.notes: Let's go through the docker run parameters one by one. rm: the container is deleted when it exits, leaving no clutter. entrypoint followed by an empty string: clears the image's default entrypoint; what happens without it, you'll see on the next page. user 1000 colon 1000: run as a normal user, so the artifacts don't end up owned by root. shm-size 15g: leave the container enough shared memory. The v parameter mounts the working directory, so the host and the container see the same path. The w parameter: after the container starts, you are already in that directory. With an NVIDIA graphics card, you can add gpus all to hand the card to the container for acceleration; this is not a required parameter for the S series. The same version also has a CPU image; for PTQ the CPU image is enough, and there's no need to add gpus all. Finally, bash -c: what's in the quotes after it is the command to run. Want to go in interactively and type commands? Replace bash -c and the command after it with bash, and add the i and t parameters. i keeps the input open, and t allocates a terminal, so it feels like logging into a machine. This recording uses one-shot commands; the effect is the same, and the logs are easier to save.

slides.title: Error 126
slides.heading: A common error: ==126==

note.p: The default entrypoint takes bash as an argument

blocks.label: ② With --entrypoint set to an empty string

lines.text: → hb_mapper starts printing its version · EXIT_CODE=0

note.p: Hit on our very first attempt

slides.notes: Now, a common mistake. This was our first attempt: the command had no entrypoint. The result: bash reports cannot execute binary file, exit code 126. The reason is that the image has a default entrypoint of its own, and our bash was handed to it as an argument. The fix: add entrypoint with an empty string. Run it again and it works: hb_mapper starts printing its version, exit code 0.

slides.notes: The first step of setting up is to open the conversion directory of the Model Zoo repository. First, the repository version: commit 7a97c17. Under samples, vision, resnet, there are conversion, evaluator, model, and runtime, plus test data and tests. Everything conversion needs is in the conversion directory. It has five files: a Chinese and an English README, export.py, ptq_x5.yaml, and ptq_s.yaml. The Chinese README has nine sections in all, going from the source model all the way to the artifacts. Directory layout, toolchain, export, calibration, compilation, and validation after conversion: this lesson walks through every one of them. These files are the Sample we use for conversion in this lesson.
slides.lead: README_cn has nine sections: model · export · calibration · compile · validation …

slides.title: export.py
slides.heading: ==export.py==: a ten-line entry point

note.p: No logic of its own; it references the shared workflow

blocks.label: ② What the README says it does

lines.text: Checks the weights hash · strict load · simplifies the graph
Two real images: logits and Top-5 compared with PyTorch

note.p: Checkpoint → ONNX is already packaged

slides.notes: First, export.py, ten lines in all. It has no logic of its own; it just references the shared workflow. The last line: the default command is export, which exports ONNX. The README says it checks the weights' hash, loads them strictly, and then simplifies the graph. It also compares logits and Top-5 against PyTorch, using two real images. The comparison error is recorded in export.json. In other words, from the checkpoint to ONNX, this step is already packaged.

slides.title: ptq_x5.yaml
slides.heading: ==ptq_x5.yaml==: the X5 template

lines.text: # Compile parameters used for the release artifacts

note.p: Only two placeholders
5 lines contain @ (comments included)
mean × 255; scale = 1 ÷ (255 × std)

slides.notes: Next, ptq_x5.yaml, the compile configuration for the X5. The comment at the top says it clearly: these are the compile parameters used for the release artifacts. Only two placeholders, @WORK@ and @SIZE@, need to be replaced by us. work is the working directory; it appears in the model path, the working directory, and the calibration data directory. size is the input size; it appears in input_shape. Normalization is already compiled into the model: the mean times 255, and the scale is 1 divided by 255 times the standard deviation. The other fields are explained section by section in the next part.
slides.lead: The X5 template in the Model Zoo repository's conversion directory (31 lines).

slides.title: ptq_s.yaml
slides.heading: ==ptq_s.yaml== vs. the X5 template
slides.lead: Shared by S100 / S100P / S600 · @TARGET@ @MARCH@ @WORK@ @SIZE@ · 46 lines (X5: 31).
head: ptq_x5.yaml
ptq_s.yaml
rows: Absent; uses a jobs / cache group instead
slides.notes: Next is ptq_s.yaml, the configuration for the S series. The S100, S100P, and S600 all share this one file. The comment lists four placeholders: @TARGET@, @MARCH@, @WORK@, and @SIZE@. target is the target name; march is nash-e, nash-m, or nash-p. Compare the two templates with diff, and the differences are visible at a glance. First, the march differs: the X5 fixes bayes-e, while for the S series it is decided by a placeholder. Second, the S series has a batch of extra default-value fields, such as debug_mode and output_nodes. Third, the S series adds std_value and separate_batch, and also quant_config. Fourth, the optimization level: O3 on the X5, O2 on the S series. Fifth, the X5 has input_source, and the S series doesn't; it uses the jobs and cache group instead.

slides.title: Calibration Data
slides.heading: Calibration data: ==two formats==

scene.text: 602,112 bytes each · the loader then converts to NV12

scene.label: S100 · .npy
scene.sub: normalized to the ONNX input · float32

steps.caption: Calibration data: a fixed set of 200 images
Preprocess first: short side to 235, center crop 224
X5: stores raw RGB; the loader converts it to NV12
S100: stores npy that is already normalized
Two targets, two formats: do not mix them up

slides.notes: Now the calibration data. The tool needs a batch of representative inputs. The Sample's recipe is fixed: 200 images. The short side is first resized to 235, then center-cropped to 224. Note that the two targets write out different data. The X5 stores the raw 0-to-255 RGB, which the loader then converts to NV12. Each one is 602,112 bytes. The S100 stores npy files that are already normalized to the ONNX input. Each one has an extra 128 bytes of file header.

slides.title: Calibration Essentials
slides.heading: Calibration ==matches deployment==
slides.lead: This lesson's calibration images: one shard of the COCO dataset on Hugging Face, 200 fixed picks; not checked against the release artifacts' calibration images.

cards.title: Same geometry
cards.text: Resize and crop the same way as at runtime.

cards.title: Same color format
cards.text: X5 stores RGB first; the loader converts to NV12.

cards.title: Same place for normalization
cards.text: X5 normalizes inside the model; S100's data is already normalized.

slides.notes: The calibration data has three key points, all about matching the deployment. The geometry must match: resize and crop the same way as at runtime. The color format must match: for the X5, RGB first, then NV12. The place where normalization happens must match too. The X5's calibration data is not normalized, because the model does it internally; the S100's is already normalized. If they don't match, the quantization parameters won't be accurate. In addition, this lesson's calibration images come from one shard of COCO on Hugging Face. They were not checked against the calibration images of the release artifacts.

slides.title: Chapter 04
slides.heading: YAML and Compilation
slides.sub: The YAML section by section, then checker, makertbin and hb_compile
slides.notes: Part four: YAML and compilation.

slides.title: X5 YAML (1/2)
slides.heading: X5 YAML: ==model and input==

note.p: march corresponds to the X5's BPU
The tool compiles the color conversion into the model
mean × 255; scale = 1 ÷ (255 × std)

slides.notes: Now let's go through the X5's YAML section by section. First section, model_parameters: the model itself. onnx_model is the exported model.onnx; march is bayes-e, which corresponds to the X5's BPU. working_dir is the artifact output directory; output_model_file_prefix decides the file name prefix, here resnet_x5. Second section, input_parameters: how the input is handled. input_name is data, matching the ONNX input name. input_type_rt is nv12: what the board feeds the model is NV12. input_type_train is rgb: during training the model took RGB, and the tool compiles the conversion into the model. input_shape is 1x3x224x224, and the layout is NCHW. norm_type uses data_mean_and_scale: subtract the mean first, then multiply by the scale. mean_value is the ImageNet mean times 255; scale_value is 1 divided by 255 times the standard deviation. input_space_and_range is bt601_video, which corresponds to the limited range of NV12.

slides.title: X5 YAML (2/2)
slides.heading: X5 YAML: ==calibration and compile==

note.p: default = automatic search
pyramid: the input comes from the board's NV12 path

slides.notes: Third section, calibration_parameters: calibration. cal_data_dir points to the 200 files we prepared. cal_data_type is float32, matching the rgb files. calibration_type is set to default, which means automatic search; an animation later explains it. preprocess_on is false: the data is already prepared, so the tool doesn't need to process the images. Fourth section, compiler_parameters: compilation. optimize_level is O3; the larger the number, the more optimization. compile_mode is latency, aiming for low latency. core_num is 1, so it uses only one core. In input_source, data is set to pyramid: the input comes from the board's NV12 image path. Put the four sections together, and you have a complete conversion configuration.

slides.title: Calibration Methods
slides.heading: default means ==automatic search==

scene.text: Same setting, but the two toolchains can choose different methods

steps.caption: calibration_type is written as default
Not skipping calibration, but an automatic search
The tool tries a set of candidates
Target: similarity 0.995
Candidate 1: two methods, max or kl
Candidate 2: percentile 0.99995 or 1.0
Candidate 3: per_channel tried on and off
Candidate 3: asymmetric also tried on and off
X5 chose max-percentile, percentile 0.99995
S100 chose kl, num_bin 1024
Same setting, but the chosen method can differ

slides.notes: In the yaml, calibration_type is written as default. This isn't doing nothing; it is an automatic search. The tool tries a set of candidates. The target similarity is 0.995. Candidate one: two methods, max or kl. Candidate two: the percentile, 0.99995 or 1.0. Candidate three: per_channel and asymmetric, each tried on and off. The results differ: the X5 chose max-percentile, with percentile 0.99995. The S100 chose kl, with num_bin 1024. With the same setting, the chosen method can be different. The details are left for the next lesson.

slides.title: S100 YAML Differences
slides.heading: The S100's YAML: ==how it differs from the X5's==
slides.lead: The S100 configuration actually used, compared item by item with the X5 configuration.
head: X5
S100
slides.notes: Now the S100's YAML, and how it differs from the X5's. march is nash-e, and the prefix is resnet_s100. There are some extra fields left blank: debug_mode, output_nodes, remove_node_name, and so on; the defaults are fine. In the input section there are an extra std_value and separate_batch, also left at their defaults. The calibration section has no preprocess_on; it has quant_config instead, left blank. The compile optimization level is O2, and there is no input_source. There is an extra jobs, with the value 16, which controls the parallelism. The S series log gives deprecation warnings for a few fields, and we'll see them in the log shortly.

slides.title: X5 checker
slides.heading: X5: ==hb_mapper checker==

note.p: Measured 5.7 s

blocks.label: ② What to look for in the log

lines.text: Versions → input ONNX → optimize → calibrate → quantize → compile
checker: 1 sample, fixed thresholds; FPS 241.75 is only an estimate
Node table: convolutions all on BPU (int8); last Reshape on CPU

note.p: The similarity column is --; checker does not compute similarity

slides.notes: The configuration is ready, so let's compile. First, the X5's checker. It is still docker run into the container; the second half is the real command: hb_mapper checker. model-type is onnx, march is bayes-e, and then the model path and the input size. After Enter, the log starts to scroll. It first prints the versions: hbdk 3.49.15, horizon_nn 1.1.0, hb_mapper 1.24.3. Then the input ONNX information: opset 11, input data, output logits. Next, in order: optimize the model, calibrate, quantize, compile, each with a start and an end. The checker's calibration uses only one sample and fixed thresholds; its purpose is only to check, so we don't look at the similarity. The compile step estimates the performance: FPS 241.75, latency 4136.5 microseconds, only an estimate. Finally the node table: every convolution layer is on the BPU, computing in int8. Only the last reshape lands on the CPU. The similarity column is just dashes; the checker doesn't compute similarity. There is no error, the exit code is 0, and the check passes.

slides.title: X5 makertbin
slides.heading: X5: ==hb_mapper makertbin==

note.p: Calibrate + quantize + compile

lines.text: Versions → read data (200, batch 8) → calibrate → quantize → compile

note.p: The waiting progress bar is played sped up

lines.text: Convert to runtime bin file successfully!
32.8 s in all · exit code 0 · resnet_x5.bin

note.p: Times are measured

slides.notes: The checker passed, so next is makertbin, the real conversion. The first half of the command is unchanged; the second half is now hb_mapper makertbin, with config.yaml as the argument. It starts with the versions and the yaml check. There is one warning: the calibration directory suffix doesn't match cal_data_type; the parameter takes precedence, so we can ignore it. Then it reads the calibration data: the name of the first image and its md5 are both printed. Next comes Horizon NN Model Convert, which covers the stages we talked about earlier. This time, calibration uses 200 samples, with a batch of 8. The calibration settings are the same as we described: max and kl, percentile, similarity 0.995. Calibration takes tens of seconds, and the screen shows a progress bar; the waiting part we play sped up. Finally it selects max-percentile, with percentile 0.99995. Then quantization, and then compilation: this time, the compiler's estimated FPS is 428.67. Next, the node table and the output similarity: the cosine similarity of logits is 0.999941. Last, the summary of the model information, including march, input type, mean, and scale. The last line: Convert to runtime bin file successfully, 32.8 seconds in all, exit code 0.

slides.title: S100: This Step Runs on CPU
slides.heading: S100: ==this step runs on CPU==

note.p: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES not set

lines.text: After calibration starts, onnxruntime errors: HzCalibration

note.p: On this machine this step did not get to use the GPU

blocks.label: ③ Forcing the CPU also runs through

lines.text: Forced onto CPU: runs all the way through · PTQ needs no GPU

note.p: Run again on the next page; the same-version CPU image also works

slides.notes: Now the S100. First, the log from a run where we did not force the CPU. The command is docker run with gpus all, and inside is hb_compile, with config.yaml as the argument. The earlier part of the log is all normal: hbdk 4.7.5, hmct 2.6.5, hb_compile 3.5.3. The calibration data is 200 images, and march is nash-e. At the calibration step, onnxruntime reports an error, and the log says ERROR. The error happens in build_model, with exit code 255, and no hbm is produced. On this machine, this step did not get to use the GPU. Set the environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to minus one to force the CPU, and it runs all the way through. This shows exactly that PTQ does not depend on a GPU.

slides.title: S100 hb_compile
slides.heading: S100: ==the full hb_compile log==

note.p: Measured 217.5 s

lines.text: Versions · yaml · warnings → 200 images → nash-e · opset 11 → 19
CUDA failure / EP Error: CPU fallback, 14 times; no effect on result
Selected kl · num_bin 1024 → quantize → per-node similarity table
compile model (~170 s, sped up) → Successfully compile the hbm model

note.p: Estimated FPS 2430.87 · latency 411.4 µs

lines.text: Inputs data_y + data_uv · output logits · exit code 0

note.p: resnet_s100.hbm

slides.notes: With CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set to minus one, let's run it again. The command has just this one extra parameter, and is otherwise the same as before. It starts with the versions and the yaml check. There are a few warnings: norm_type and cal_data_type are deprecated, and using them as in the Sample is fine. Then it reads the calibration data: 200 images, and the md5 of the first one is printed too. Next is Horizon NN Model Convert, with march nash-e. The input ONNX is opset 11, and the tool converts it to opset 19. Now the calibration settings: two methods, max and kl, percentiles 0.99995 and 1.0, and a target similarity of 0.995. Calibration starts. Lots of CUDA failure and EP Error messages appear on screen. These are the messages from the container trying the GPU without success and automatically falling back to the CPU, 14 times in all. They don't affect the result, and calibration keeps going. Calibration finishes, and kl is selected, with num_bin 1024. Next it quantizes, exports the model, and then checks the parameters. Then comes the node-by-node similarity table: every layer's cosine similarity after calibration is above 0.98. The last table is logits: 0.999913 after calibration, and 0.999856 after quantization. Then it enters compile model, the slowest step, about 170 seconds as measured, and we play it sped up. Successfully compile the hbm model appears, and the compile succeeds. The compiler's estimated FPS is 2430.87, again only an estimate. Finally it prints the model information: march is nash-e, plus the memory use of each part. There are two inputs, data_y and data_uv, and this is the split NV12. The output is logits. The last line: hb_compile completes running, 217.5 seconds in all, exit code 0.

slides.notes: With the compile done, let's look at the artifacts. In the X5's build directory, resnet_x5.bin is the final artifact, 11,081,570 bytes. The onnx files beside it correspond to each step of the flow: original, optimized, calibrated, quantized. quant_info.json records the quantization information for each node, and the html and json files are the compile reports. Use sha256 to note the artifact's fingerprint; the bin starts with 7f8fa575. In the S100's build directory, resnet_s100.hbm is 12,193,304 bytes. There are also two csv files, advice and node_info, a bc file, and hb_compile.log. The hbm's sha256 starts with a506767b. Now open quant_info: one entry per node, 50 entries in all. Look at the fc node: thresholds is 3.865509, and cosine_similarity is 0.999941. This similarity matches the logits line in the log. The S100 is the same: thresholds is 2.823619, and the similarity is 0.999913. The two sides use different definitions, so we don't compare which is bigger.

slides.notes: After conversion, look at the similarity first. The S100 log has two columns. Calibrated is the cosine between the float model and the calibrated model: 0.999913. Quantized is the cosine between the float model and the quantized fixed-point model: 0.999856. The X5 has only one column. It is the cosine between the float model and the quantized model: 0.999941. The two sides use different definitions, so don't compare which is better. An output-node similarity below 0.8 usually means an obvious accuracy loss. It is only a reference; in the end, what counts is the task accuracy.

slides.title: How Evaluation Works
slides.heading: How ==evaluation== works

scene.text: Top-1: first place = label  ·  Top-5: label is among the top 5

steps.caption: Data: ImageNetV2 MatchedFrequency
Not the ILSVRC2012 val set; the numbers cannot be compared with each other
Preprocessing: resize, crop to 224
Model: outputs 1000 scores
Top-K: sort the scores, take the top 5
Top-1: first place is the label; Top-5: the label is in the top 5
Statistics: Top-1 and Top-5
On the computer, evaluate.py evaluates the float ONNX
On the board, evaluate_board.py evaluates the bin or hbm

slides.notes: Stage five, evaluation. Evaluation means comparing accuracy on a dataset, and the pipeline has five steps: data, preprocessing, model, take the top few, and statistics. The data is the MatchedFrequency set of ImageNetV2: ten thousand images, one thousand classes. Note that it is not the ILSVRC 2012 validation set, so the numbers cannot be compared with that set's. Preprocessing is resize and crop to 224, with the same rule on both paths. The model gives one thousand scores, which are sorted to take the top five. If the first place equals the label, it counts as Top-1 correct; if the label is among the top five, it counts as Top-5 correct. The statistic is the proportion of correct images out of the total. On the PC, evaluate.py evaluates the float ONNX. On the board, evaluate_board.py evaluates the bin or hbm.

slides.title: Five Rules
slides.heading: The ==five rules== of conversion
slides.lead: When it will not run, or the numbers do not match, check these five first.

items.text: PTQ runs on the CPU alone; a GPU is only an optional speed-up; CUDA messages in the log can be ignored
Switching board types means converting again (S100P uses nash-m)
Verify with Top-1 and the order of magnitude of the scores

slides.notes: Finally, five rules. One, the image needs an empty entrypoint, otherwise you get 126. Two, PTQ can be done on the CPU alone, and the GPU is only an optional speed-up; the CUDA messages in the log can be ignored. Three, the calibration preprocessing must match the deployment. Four, artifacts are compiled per board type, and switching board types means converting again. The S100P needs a separate conversion with nash-m. Five, for verification, look at Top-1 and the order of magnitude of the scores.
